title: The Hajj caravans
hook: caravans from Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad carried pilgrims and the new cover for the Ka'ba

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eid around the world: Lebaran, Bayram, Sallah, and one greeting, Eid Mubarak. Your line was eid in every language. Which greeting did you learn? Day one thousand forty-five.

Bells first, then dust. A long line of camels sways out under a city gate before sunrise, bells at their necks. Curtained litters on their backs, riders swaying inside. Water skins, sacks of grain, guards on horseback, a doctor, a judge, merchants hoping to trade along the way. People line the road to watch them go, some in tears, because the road is long and hard. Some days back we stood in a terminal at Jeddah, with pilgrims a day from home. Before the planes and the ships, this is how the Hajj began. Today: the Hajj caravans.
screen: `BELLS, THEN DUST.` → `OUT OF THE CITY GATE.` → `BEFORE THE PLANES.`

segments.voice: First, the duty and its condition. At the Jeddah terminal we heard the verse that makes the pilgrimage owed "for him who can find a way thither." Then the way was a flight. Here, look at what the same words asked of a pilgrim in the caravan centuries: finding a way meant a road, and a road meant company. You did not cross the desert alone. Second, the great cities. Caravans gathered in Cairo, in Damascus, in Baghdad, and set out together on fixed routes. A caravan was led by an appointed commander of the pilgrimage, the amir al-hajj, whose job was to keep the people fed, watered, guarded, and moving. The traveler Ibn Battuta, from Morocco, wrote of going to Mecca with the caravan from Damascus. Third, the road itself. Along the route from Iraq ran a line of wells and cisterns, and tradition credits Zubayda, the wife of the caliph Harun al-Rashid, whom we met earlier this year, with paying for many of them, so the road still carries her name. Water, in the desert, was the gift that let a pilgrim live to pray. Fourth, what rode along. From Cairo and Damascus, a richly decorated empty litter, the mahmal, traveled with the caravan as a sign of the ruler's care for the pilgrims. And from Cairo, the caravan carried something for the House itself, a new cloth for the Ka'ba. More on that tomorrow. The Qur'an pictures pilgrims coming on foot and on lean camels, "from every deep ravine." Behind each of those ravines was a road, and people who kept it open.
screen: `FOR HIM WHO CAN FIND A WAY.` · `CAIRO, DAMASCUS, BAGHDAD.` · `ZUBAYDA'S WELLS ON THE ROAD.` · `THE MAHMAL AND A NEW CLOTH.` · then, large: `THE LONG ROAD TO MECCA.`

segments.voice: The practice: travel the long road in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture yourself at a city gate before sunrise, your bags tied on a camel. Feel the first hour, the slow sway, the sun coming up over sand. Then the long middle: heat, thirst, a well at evening, strangers becoming companions around a fire. Don't hurry it. Notice how far it is, step after step. Then, at last, someone up ahead calls out, and the road bends toward Mecca. If you pray, you can remember everyone who ever walked that road, and those who never arrived. If not, simply honor the distance. The bell holds the time.
Mahmal, the empty, richly decorated litter that traveled with a Hajj caravan as a sign of the ruler's care for the pilgrims on the long road to Mecca. Today's word.
Your line: the long road to mecca. Today, on any slow stretch, a commute, a queue, a long walk, remember the caravans and travel it without complaint. Day one thousand forty-five.

howItsDone: Today pilgrims travel to Mecca in organized groups, by air, sea or road, often led by a guide, which carries on the caravan's habit of making the journey together.

what it means: a whole traveling town of pilgrims, guarded and supplied on the road to Mecca.

notes: Claims rule: no numbers of pilgrims, distances or journey lengths are given.
